title: Unitary RQL Equals RQL
abstract: Intermediate measurements let quantum computations discard information and reuse their workspace. Deferring all measurements can require storing their entire history, which need not preserve logarithmic space. Fefferman and Remscrim proved that measurements can nevertheless be eliminated with two-sided bounded error, and asked whether the same holds with one-sided error [FR21]. We prove RQLΓ = RQULΓ for the standard gate set Γ = {H, T, CNOT}, preserving polynomial time, logarithmic space, and exactly zero acceptance on no-instances. Our proof extends the density-matrix doubling method of Girish, Raz and Zhan [ GRZ21 ] to general channels, including resets and classical memory. We also prove measurement elimination for broader finite gate sets with exact inverses, including suitable gates with transcendental entries, and establish gate-set independence for a specified family of algebraic gate sets. A separate history-checking construction proves QMAL1,G = QUMAL1,G under explicit gate assumptions: measurements can also be eliminated from logarithmic-space quantum verification while preserving perfect completeness
summary: This paper tackles the theoretical question of whether intermediate measurements are necessary in quantum computation when operating under limited resources like logarithmic space. The authors prove that for standard gate sets, measurements can be eliminated while maintaining computational power, extending known techniques to general channels and quantum verification settings.
main_problem: The central problem is determining if intermediate measurements in quantum computation can be eliminated while preserving computational power, specifically addressing the one-sided error case ($	ext{RQL} = 	ext{RQUL}$).
main_result: The authors prove that $	ext{RQL}_{\Gamma} = 	ext{RQUL}_{\Gamma}$ for the standard gate set $\Gamma$, preserving polynomial time, logarithmic space, and zero acceptance on no-instances.
method: The proof extends the density-matrix doubling method to general channels and utilizes a history-checking construction for quantum verification.
model_or_system: The work analyzes quantum computation models ($	ext{RQL}$, $	ext{RQUL}$) operating in polynomial time with logarithmic space, using gate sets like $\Gamma = \{	ext{H}, 	ext{T}, 	ext{CNOT}\}$ as the underlying computational resource.
key_observables: Acceptance probability (must be exactly zero on no-instances), computational space ($	ext{O}(\log n)$), and time complexity (polynomial).
important_parameters: The error type (two-sided vs. one-sided) and the specific gate set $\Gamma$ or $	ext{G}$ used for the computation.
main_assumptions: The proof relies on the established two-sided measurement-elimination theorem and assumes specific conditions on the gate sets (e.g., exact inverses or entries in a fixed CM field).
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes prior complexity results; Figure 2 details the direct simulation process involving reweighting and unitary circuits; Figure 3 illustrates the factorization of the simulation into algebraic and unitary components.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the core measurement elimination result ($	ext{RQL} = 	ext{RQUL}$), then detailing the simulation construction using reweighting and unitary circuits, and finally extending these results to broader gate sets and quantum verification settings.
why_interesting: This work provides deep theoretical insights into the resource requirements of quantum computation, particularly concerning the necessity of intermediate measurements, which is fundamental for designing efficient quantum algorithms.

The first two stages describe matrices; the last three implement the simulation in logarithmic space and polynomial time.
